svg.title: Exchange surfaces
svg.desc: Why exchange systems?: Single cells have a large surface area to volume ratio. Their outer surface can meet exchange needs. Large multicellular organisms have a lower ratio and longer diffusion distances. They need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems. Surface area : volume: Cube side a: Surface area = 6a² Volume = a³ 1 cm cube: 6 ÷ 1 = 6:1. 3 cm cube: 54 ÷ 27 = 2:1. A larger cube has more total area, but less area per unit volume. Cutting it into pieces exposes more area without changing total volume. Lung alveoli: Many tiny air sacs give a large surface area. Thin alveolar and capillary walls give a short diffusion path. Blood supply and ventilation maintain steep gradients. Oxygen: air to blood. Carbon dioxide: blood to air. An alveolus is one air sac. Small intestine: Villi and microvilli: large surface area. Thin lining: short diffusion distance. Blood removes absorbed substances, maintaining gradients. Sugars can enter blood by active transport, against a gradient. Fish gills: Many filaments and lamellae: large surface area. Thin surfaces: short diffusion distance. Blood and flowing water maintain gradients. Oxygen moves from water to blood. Carbon dioxide moves out. Plant roots: Root hairs: large contact area with soil. Water enters by osmosis through a partially permeable membrane. Minerals enter against a gradient by active transport, using respiration energy. Plant leaves: Broad: large surface area. Thin: short diffusion distance. Stomata: let gases in and out. Internal air spaces shorten diffusion paths. For photosynthesis, carbon dioxide enters and oxygen can diffuse out. Explain an adaptation: Large area: more particles cross at once. Thin barrier: shorter diffusion path. Blood supply: brings or removes substances to maintain gradients. Ventilation: refreshes air or water. Name the substance and direction. Explain how the feature makes exchange faster.
